# Retrieval practice

How to make learning stick, and why most study habits fail.

## Why re-reading fails

Re-reading feels productive because familiarity is mistaken for knowledge. The
text gets easier to scan, and that ease is read as understanding. It is not.

- Fluency illusion: recognizing a sentence is not the same as being able to
  produce it.
- The effect is strongest for the material you already know best.
- Testing after re-reading exposes the gap immediately, which is why it is
  uncomfortable.

## Why retrieval works

Pulling something out of memory changes the memory. Each successful retrieval
makes the next one easier, which is the opposite of what happens when you
merely look at the answer again.

- The difficulty of retrieval is the mechanism, not a side effect.
- Failing to retrieve, then seeing the answer, still beats passive review.
- Spacing the attempts amplifies the effect considerably.

### How to space it

Optimal spacing grows with each successful review rather than staying fixed.

- First review: within a day.
- Then roughly double the interval each time.
- When recall fails, drop back to a short interval instead of pushing forward.

## What this means in practice

- Replace the second read with a blank-page recall attempt.
- Write the question, not the answer, in your notes.
- Keep the answer on a separate line or page so it can be hidden.

## Where it breaks down

Retrieval practice is worse than re-reading when the material is brand new and
you have no partial knowledge to retrieve. In that case, read once first.
